title: Satisfied and Satisfying
hook: a cook who eats last and fills every plate, and a goddess whose open hand pours coins
carry: lakshmi's fortune is meant to flow outward
tomorrow: why do some Hindus go to Lakshmi first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hymn heard her coming, horses, a chariot, elephants, and asked only that she be pleased to be here: puja, welcoming the divine as a beloved guest.

At a big family dinner there's often one person who eats last. She's been at the stove since noon. She notices your plate is empty before you do, and fills it, and fills the next one. And when she finally sits down, she doesn't look tired so much as content, the way someone looks when they had enough to give. The Sri Sukta has a phrase for that. Today the hymn stops calling the goddess and starts describing her, and one pair of words sits right in the middle.
screen: `SHE EATS LAST.` → `SHE FILLS EVERY PLATE.` → `CONTENT, NOT TIRED.`

segments.voice: First, where she comes from. The Puranas tell that when the gods and the demons churned the ocean of milk, treasures rose out of it one by one, and then Lakshmi rose, seated on a lotus, and the whole world brightened. The Sri Sukta paints her in that light. Here's the line, in paraphrase. Smiling, within a wall of gold, moist and blazing, satisfied and satisfying, standing on the lotus, the color of the lotus: I call Sri near. Start with the strange pairing: moist and blazing. Wet and on fire at once. Some readers hear tenderness and radiance; others, the monsoon and the sun a field needs. The hymn lets her hold both. Then the pair this day is about: satisfied, and satisfying. In Sanskrit the two words echo, triptam tarpayantim. She is full, and she makes others full. Notice the order. Her fullness comes first, and the filling flows out of it. That's the cook at the dinner table: she isn't giving from an empty pot. And here's the teaching families see every Diwali. In so many pictures of Lakshmi, gold coins pour from her open hand. Her wealth isn't locked behind the gold wall; it spills. Many Hindus take that as how fortune should move through a home: what comes in goes out again, as sweets carried to the neighbors, gifts, and giving to people in need. A goddess of wealth who hoards wouldn't be Lakshmi. She's smiling, soft and bright. She has enough, and so she shares.
screen: `SHE ROSE FROM THE OCEAN OF MILK.` · `MOIST AND BLAZING AT ONCE.` · `SATISFIED, AND SATISFYING.` · `COINS POUR FROM HER HAND.` · then, large: `FULL, AND SO SHE FILLS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come in all the way, without forcing it, and go out slowly, as if you're giving it away: in until you're full, out as a gift. If a face comes to mind, someone who could use a little of what you have, let them sit with you on the out-breath, and choose one small thing to share with them this week: a sweet, a call, a little money. If you pray, you can offer them to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, just keep breathing in and giving out.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that paints Sri smiling, moist and blazing, standing on the lotus: satisfied, and satisfying.
Your line: Lakshmi's fortune is meant to flow outward. Full first, and then the filling flows. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Images of Lakshmi in homes and temples often show her seated or standing on a lotus, and the Sri Sukta's descriptions of her are chanted in front of such images during Lakshmi worship.

fork.setup: it's Diwali, and a lot has come your way this year. the Sri Sukta's goddess is satisfied and satisfying. what does that ask of you?
options: lock it up so it stays.

fork.reveal: she's full, and so she fills. in pictures her coins pour outward, and many families give at Diwali for the same reason.

notes: Verse 4 paraphrased: kāṃ sosmitāṃ hiraṇyaprākārām ārdrāṃ jvalantīṃ tṛptāṃ tarpayantīm / padmesthitāṃ padmavarṇāṃ tām ihopahvaye śriyam. 'kāṃ' is read variously (as 'her who is bliss', or as a mystic syllable); the script leaves it out. Confirm.
'The two words share a root sound' is said of tṛptāṃ / tarpayantīm (both from tṛp); stated as sound, not etymology. Confirm.
Readings of 'moist and blazing' (compassion and radiance; rain and sun) are offered as 'some readers' / 'others'; confirm they are fair.
'The lotus will come back again in this hymn' is true of later verses (padminī, padmamālinī); the iconographic remark is phrased as pictures the listener may have seen.
